mfg1-surface-lesson-050.title: Check reaction equivalents before converting concentration notation
mfg1-surface-lesson-050.objective:
Distinguish mol/L from reaction-based equivalent concentration.
Specify the reaction equation when converting.
mfg1-surface-lesson-050.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 8 on equations, 8 on the sulfuric-acid example, and 7 calculating the comparison with NaOH. Write questions about N notation in 3 minutes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-050.summary:
Specify the reaction for equivalent concentration.
Do not interchange it with mol/L by numbers alone; check factors and balances.
safety: Do not add or mix real chemicals based on learning calculations.
Do not guess conversions when reaction conditions are unknown.

paragraphs.title: Decide what the reaction counts
paragraphs.text: Molar concentration is amount of substance per solution volume. The older notation normality counts equivalents for a specified reaction. Even for the same substance, the equivalent value can change with the reaction definition, so the symbol N alone provides insufficient conditions.

paragraphs.title: Check the factor from the equation
paragraphs.text: For complete neutralization H₂SO₄+2 NaOH→Na₂SO₄+2 H₂O,1 mol sulfuric acid corresponds to 2 mol sodium hydroxide. Under these conditions,0.30 mol/L sulfuric acid is 0.60 equiv/L. Simply dividing mol/L by the acid's valence does not match this reaction balance. The original learning text contradicts its example, so do not use that sentence as a calculation rule.

paragraphs.title: Compare the method document and analysis sheet
paragraphs.text: Check conversion conditions against the reaction: electron numbers for redox, reacting hydrogen ions for neutralization, and so forth. To avoid misunderstanding, state mol/L together with the specific reaction equation. Do not simply replace N with mol/L while keeping the number; ask the responsible person about the reaction and definition.

paragraphs.title: A paper comparison
paragraphs.text: When NaOH at 0.40 mol/L is used in a one-equivalent neutralization, it is 0.40 equiv/L. Its factor differs from complete sulfuric-acid neutralization. Write both equations, compare required amounts, and explain that concentration calculation and permission to replenish an actual tank are different.

terms.meaning: A way of expressing corresponding amounts in a specified reaction.
An older notation for reaction-dependent equivalent concentration.
A number expressing the ratio of corresponding amounts of substance in a reaction equation.
Here, conditions under which both acidic hydrogens of sulfuric acid react.

mfg1-surface-lesson-051.title: Understand pH measurement with glass and reference electrodes
mfg1-surface-lesson-051.objective:
Explain electrode potential differences and the instrument's role.
Do not confuse test-paper colors with instrument readings.
mfg1-surface-lesson-051.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 8 on electrode relationships, 8 on temperature and calibration, and 7 preparing a portable-meter abnormality report. Check storage procedures in 3 minutes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-051.summary:
Use pH-meter potential differences together with measurement conditions.
Check the target and procedure for both color charts and instruments.
safety: Do not immerse an electrode in a chemical liquid of unknown instrument compatibility.
Disassembly or internal-liquid changes require designated procedures and authority.

paragraphs.title: Relate potential difference to pH
paragraphs.text: A glass-electrode pH meter uses a reference electrode to measure a potential difference associated with sample conditions and relate it to pH. A display alone does not establish suitability; check calibration, electrode condition and temperature. Internal electrode structure and liquid are model-specific, so a general diagram does not authorize disassembly or refilling.

paragraphs.title: Separate the change from its conditions
paragraphs.text: The relationship between potential difference and pH depends on conditions such as temperature. Do not treat approximately 60 mV per pH unit as an exact constant at all temperatures. Follow specifications for calibration solution and temperature, and obtain the designated inspection if abnormal.

paragraphs.title: Applications and preparation
paragraphs.text: Fixed, benchtop and portable instruments have different applications. Check sampling, cleaning, electrode storage and sample suitability through the procedure. Test-paper color charts are product-specific; do not use the textbook chart as a universal decision chart.

paragraphs.title: Record unusual instability
paragraphs.text: If a portable meter's value will not stabilize, report calibration status, electrode contamination, temperature and measurement time rather than recording only a favorable instant. The operator must not fix it by adding a different internal liquid without authorization.

terms.meaning: An electrode using a glass membrane to measure a potential related to pH.
An electrode providing a reference potential for comparison.
The difference in electric potential between two points.
A specified solution used as a reference for calibration or similar purposes.

mfg1-surface-lesson-052.title: Distinguish DC, AC and circuit symbols from diagrams
mfg1-surface-lesson-052.objective:
Distinguish conditions for current direction and magnitude.
Read symbols for resistors, capacitors, earth and power supplies.
mfg1-surface-lesson-052.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 8 on DC and AC, 8 on five symbols, and 7 reading a schematic. Write the difference between drawings and actual equipment in 3 minutes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-052.summary:
Distinguish direction from magnitude and cycles from polarity changes.
Read symbols together with connections and checks of actual equipment.
safety: Change AC/DC ranges and connections only within training and procedures.
Do not touch live parts based on an insulating material's name alone.

paragraphs.title: DC is not necessarily constant
paragraphs.text: Study DC as current flowing in one direction. Some examples are constant, but DC magnitude can also vary with time, as in pulsation after rectification. AC changes direction periodically.50 Hz means 50 cycles per second, distinct from merely counting 50 polarity changes.

paragraphs.title: Read symbols and connections together
paragraphs.text: Resistors, capacitors, earth connections, batteries and AC supplies have different symbols. Long and short battery lines help identify polarity. Follow junctions and wiring extents as well as symbols. Check drawing rules where lines cross without a connection indication.

paragraphs.title: Conductors and insulators also have conditions
paragraphs.text: Metals are typical conductors, while rubber and resins are typical insulators, but contamination, moisture, damage and voltage can change the hazard. A material name alone does not guarantee shock protection. An earth symbol on the drawing and a sound actual earth connection are also different.

paragraphs.title: Compare indications
paragraphs.text: If a drawing specifies DC but the meter is on an AC range, do not use the value directly for process decisions. Check the supply type, instrument compatibility, responsible person and procedure. Do not alter actual wiring for learning.

terms.meaning: The time for one complete repetition of a change.
Connecting equipment or similar items to earth by a specified method.

mfg1-surface-lesson-053.title: Consider current and magnetic-field directions with a stated viewpoint
mfg1-surface-lesson-053.objective:
Distinguish right-hand rules for a straight conductor and a coil.
Explain the quantities in Fleming's rules.
mfg1-surface-lesson-053.activity: Spend 4 minutes on terms, 8 on straight conductors, 8 on coils and the left hand, and 7 preparing an explanation with a viewpoint. Check left- versus right-hand uses in 3 minutes.
mfg1-surface-lesson-053.summary:
Match hand rules to quantities and viewpoints.
Distinguish straight conductors, coils, force and induction.
safety: Do not touch rotating parts or wiring to learn directions.
Do not independently energize conductors or bring in magnets.

paragraphs.title: Consider the space around a straight conductor
paragraphs.text: Current in a straight conductor creates a magnetic field around it. Point the right thumb along conventional current; the curled four fingers indicate the magnetic-field direction. Before saying clockwise, specify which side of the conductor you are viewing.

paragraphs.title: The correspondence changes for a coil
paragraphs.text: For a coil, curl the right fingers along the current's circulation and use the thumb for the internal magnetic field. Do not confuse this with the straight-conductor rule in which the thumb indicated current. Electric fields relate to charges and magnetic fields to magnets or currents; applications include motors.

paragraphs.title: Separate force from induction
paragraphs.text: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the index finger represents magnetic field, the middle finger conventional current and the thumb force. Use it for current experiencing force in a magnetic field. In the right-hand rule, the index finger represents magnetic field, the middle finger induced current and the thumb conductor motion. Use motion and field to consider induced-current direction. Do not swap hands; align the phenomenon and viewpoint.

paragraphs.title: Check directions on paper
paragraphs.text: Mark the viewpoint and current arrows on a diagram. Explain the right-hand rules for straight conductors and coils and the left-hand motor rule separately. There is no need to touch a running motor or wiring to copy a hand position.

terms.meaning: A field of force associated with magnets or currents.
The current direction defined by the movement of positive charge.
Current produced by changes in the relationship with a magnetic field or similar effects.
